text:
*Interview with Madame Odile Monnier, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Madame, I am sorry to keep you from your rest on such a night. I must ask you about your husband and about the evening. Take your time. First, tell me your place in this household.

MME MONNIER: I am Aurèle Monnier's wife. I have been his wife for thirty years and I have kept his house for thirty years. Write that down, Inspector. It is all the place I have.

MATTHEY: Did you go up to the atelier often?

MME MONNIER: No. His work was his own. I knew the sound of his bench from the salon, and I knew his face when a watch had gone wrong. A wife learns no more than that about such a trade.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the dinner.

MME MONNIER: We sat down as we do every year. When the temple bell struck nine, my husband made us all take out our watches. He does it every year. He tells each owner what is wrong with his watch, and he enjoys it more than the owner does.

MATTHEY: And what did he say to Félix?

MME MONNIER: Félix's watch showed twenty minutes to nine. My husband scolded him for it in front of the table. Félix laughed, as he does when he is put out. You will have noticed that Félix laughs a great deal.

MATTHEY: Was there any other disagreement at the table?

MME MONNIER: Monsieur Girard and my husband quarrelled about the price of the repeater. Monsieur Girard wished to buy the rights to it, and my husband would not sell them for what he was offered. It was not the first quarrel between them, and I do not suppose it will be the last.

MATTHEY: Do you know of Félix's affairs?

MME MONNIER: He owes money. Some of it is owed to Monsieur Girard. I do not know how much, and I have never asked. Félix is my late brother-in-law's son, and this house has been generous to him. I think he has taken that generosity for granted.

MATTHEY: What did you do later in the evening?

MME MONNIER: We went into the salon. When the temple struck ten, I looked at the salon clock. It showed five minutes to ten.

MATTHEY: And then?

MME MONNIER: Casimir and I played piquet. Casimir Vauthier is the family's doctor. He has been my husband's friend since they were young men, and he is the oldest friend this house has. We played without a break until he said he must fetch his cigars. He went out at twenty-eight minutes past ten by the salon clock.

MATTHEY: Did he say anything more as he went?

MME MONNIER: He asked me to play for him. I sat down at the piano at once and played until he came back, and I stopped when he came in. I played Chopin. Casimir likes Chopin, and it is the music I play best.

MATTHEY: Did he speak to you when he came back?

MME MONNIER: A moment after he came back, the hall clock struck eleven.

MATTHEY: You have not asked me how your husband died.

MME MONNIER: I have not. You will tell me what you choose to tell me. I was married to him for thirty years, Inspector, and my love for him was worn smooth long ago, like the step at the foot of our stairs. People expect a wife to weep in front of a policeman. I do not weep in front of anyone.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Madame. I ask only that you remain in the house until I have seen the others.

MME MONNIER: Where else would I go?
